text:
In the autumn of her third year at the college—a cluster of mock-Gothic buildings tucked into the damp hills of western Massachusetts—Clara took a top-floor room in a house painted the color of spoiled mustard. Her housemates were four: Lizzy, who had attended a Quaker boarding school and wore only oatmeal-colored knits; Martin, a minor diplomat’s son whose accent shifted depending on his beverage; Carl, an architectural theory student who spent evenings building useless balsa-wood bridges; and Johan, an exchange student from Uppsala who had arrived with a single canvas rucksack and an air of profound, almost offensive calm.

They were, Clara realized by mid-October, an ecosystem designed for miniature catastrophes.

At twenty, Clara was still assembling a personality from the spare parts of books she had read and people she envied. Raised in a Cleveland suburb that smelled perpetually of wet pavement and lawn fertilizer, she was determined to become someone who knew what to do with an artichoke. In the evenings, they gathered in the kitchen, where the linoleum peeled in curling continents, drinking three-dollar wine from mustard jars and discussing the impending collapse of late capitalism.

Carl claimed her first, though "claimed" was too active a verb for Carl. He simply began leaving French structuralist translations outside her door, margins filled with his microscopic handwriting. *Thought of you,* a scrap of paper would say, tucked beside a twice-underlined passage about the alienation of the modern pedestrian. 

Carl was tall and stooped, with the pale complexion of a cellar tuber. When she returned his books, he would be hunched over his drafting table, an X-Acto knife clenched between his teeth, the floor littered with wood shavings that stuck to her wool socks.

"You're the only one here who actually listens, Clara," he told her one soggy November Tuesday, gesturing toward the clanking radiator with his knife. "Martin performs. Lizzy absorbs. Johan—God knows what Johan is doing. Digesting, probably. Wait until February. A house this size can't support four distinct egos."

"There are five of us," Clara pointed out from the edge of his bare mattress.

"You don't have an ego yet," Carl said, smiling in a way that made her feel simultaneously insulted and entirely understood. "You're still in the preliminary sketching phase."

They began an affair conducted entirely in whispers, because secrecy was the only way Carl knew how to generate heat. In his room, smelling of rubber cement and sour wool, Clara felt she was participating in something deeply European and slightly tragic. He was not a generous lover; he approached her body like a municipal zoning problem to be solved before dawn. Afterward, she climbed to her attic bed feeling a strange, hollow triumph she mistook for sophistication.

Lizzy noticed first, because Lizzy noticed everything, usually while washing someone else’s frying pan.

"He's very fragile, you know," Lizzy said before Thanksgiving, sorting bruised apples in the pantry, her weak-tea hair pinned with chopsticks. "Last year, when a cellist from the conservatory broke it off, he stayed in the bathtub for thirty-six hours. Martin had to read him *The Magic Mountain* through the keyhole just to get him to pull the plug."

"We aren't anything," Clara said, resenting Lizzy’s serene maternal authority. "We just talk about Foucault."

"Of course," Lizzy said mildly. "It’s just that Carl makes people feel responsible for his structural integrity. And you have such a nice face, Clara. It would be a shame if it got all pinched."

The warning made Clara feel her arrangement with Carl was a grand passion fraught with peril. Yet, as the first gray snow fell, her attention drifted toward Martin.

If Carl was a basement, Martin was a conservatory full of mirrors. He studied political science, wrote vitriolic letters to the student paper under pseudonyms, and wore a velvet smoking jacket over frayed jeans.

"The problem with Carl," Martin said in early December, when the others were at a lecture, "is that he thinks misery is an aesthetic. Have some gin. I bought it from a man in a Pittsfield parking lot."

They sat before the fireplace, burning old *New York Reviews of Books* because nobody had ordered cordwood. The paper burned with a frantic, green-edged flame that gave off no heat.

"Carl is very serious," Clara said loyally, taking the mustard jar of gin.

"Carl is a tourist in his own gloom," Martin said, eyes dark as wet coal. "You, however, are a romantic. I can tell by the way you cut your bread. Very thick, very uneven. A person who believes in sustenance."

"That just means I'm bad with a bread knife."

"Everything is a metaphor, darling, if you're bored enough," Martin said, tucking hair behind her ear with warm fingers that smelled of clove cigarettes.

Where Carl treated her as an apprentice, Martin treated her as a co-conspirator. Soon, they shared a private language of glances across the dinner table. Too cowardly to risk Carl’s thirty-six-hour bathtub vigil, Clara began dividing her nights. She would watch Carl glue basswood until midnight, plead exhaustion, climb toward the attic, and slip into Martin’s room on the second-floor landing.

With Martin, love was a theatrical production. He recited Auden while she was half-asleep; he bit her shoulder and apologized in French.

"We are terrible people," she whispered once at six a.m.

"We're young," Martin corrected, kissing her collarbone. "Morality is for people with mortgages."

Into the bone-cracking January cold, Johan remained at the periphery—a tall, blond smudge studying forestry, spending afternoons walking the state forest in enormous rubberized boots. He spoke meticulous, archaic English and was the only one who cleaned the stove’s grease trap. 

Sometimes, descending from Martin’s room at dawn, her mouth tasting of cloves and cheap gin, Clara found Johan in the kitchen drinking black coffee, watching the bird feeder he had nailed to the clothesline post.

"Good morning, Clara," he would say, never glancing at the stairs or her bare feet. "The chickadees are very aggressive today. The pressure is dropping."

She found his lack of curiosity about her inner life mildly insulting. He simply poured her coffee, pushed the milk across the scarred Formica, and watched the birds.

The collapse came on a Thursday in late February, during a thaw that filled the gutters with rushing, dirty water. Clara came home early from a seminar, took off her wet boots in the vestibule, and walked down the hall in damp socks. She stopped by the coat rack outside the kitchen, arrested by her own name.

"It’s a classic Midwest narrative," Martin was saying, his voice bright, clipped, and conversational. "She’s desperately trying to acquire patina. You’re the intellectual credential, Carl, and I’m the continental corruption. Honestly, it’s rather sweet. Like watching a kitten try to smoke a cigar."

There was the wet *schlump* of Lizzy stirring soup.

"She thinks I don't know," Carl said, sounding amused rather than fragile. "She comes into my room smelling of your ridiculous Indonesian cigarettes. Yesterday she tried to explain my own thesis to me using a violin metaphor she clearly lifted from your *Review* essay."

"Did she really?" Martin laughed. "God, the earnestness. Though she is tidy. Always makes the bed before sneaking back to the attic."

"Boys," Lizzy said, and Clara felt a desperate flare of hope. "Leave her alone. She’s just trying to keep up. You know how it is when they come from public schools in Ohio. They think everything is a novel."

"It is a novel," Martin said cheerfully. "A minor one. Regional fiction. Pass the salt, Liz."

Clara stood by the coats for a long time, feeling a dizzying weightlessness, as if the floor had turned to glass. She didn't make a scene; she knew that would only provide Martin with an anecdote. Instead, she walked backward down the hall, put on her wet boots, and went out.

She walked for two hours along Route 2 as logging trucks roared past, throwing up brown slush. She thought of practicing her laugh in the mirror to sound less like her mother; of spending thirty-five dollars on Walter Benjamin just to leave it on the coffee table; of Carl’s X-Acto knife, and Martin watching his reflection in the window while kissing her. She wasn't a person at all, she realized. She was a series of auditions.

When she returned at dusk, Billie Holiday records drifted from the dining room. Intending to use the back servants' stairs, she went around to the mudroom. 

Johan sat on the back steps under the yellow porch light, rubbing grease from a tin of dubbin into his boots with an old flannel rag. He looked up at her slush-caked coat and dry, wide eyes.

"You missed the chickadees," he said, continuing his circular motion. "And a nuthatch."

Clara stopped, shivering so hard her teeth clicked. "They were talking about me," she said, her voice flat and Ohioan. "In the kitchen."

Johan nodded, inspecting the boot welt. "They talk about everyone. Last week, Martin explained I am a mild autist because I dislike his poetry. Before that, Carl said Lizzy is in love with her brother." He picked up the other boot. "It is how they stay warm. Like burning newspapers in the grate. A lot of light for two minutes, then just dirt on the rug."

Clara sat on the wet bottom step. "I thought we were all in it together."

"Nobody is in anything together here," Johan said mildly. "Except perhaps the pantry mice. Your feet are wet. Come inside. They are in the front room arguing about Godard."

In the warm kitchen, Johan ignored the rusty mustard jars, putting the kettle on and dropping teabags into two chipped ceramic mugs. Clara sat with her hands flat on the peeling linoleum, listening to Martin’s sharp bark of laughter through the wall.

"I don't even like Foucault," she told the salt shaker. "I just liked the way the paper smelled."

Johan poured the boiling water and sat opposite her. "My grandfather was a carpenter in Gävle. He said if you build a chair to impress the neighbors, nobody can sit in it without their spine hurting. You have been trying to build a very strange chair, Clara."

She looked at him properly for the first time—at the small scar on his chin, his pale winter-sky eyes. There was no irony in his face, no hidden mirror.

"What do I do now?" she asked. Twelve weeks remained on the lease.

"Drink your tea," Johan said. "Take off your wet stockings. Tomorrow, I am going to the reservoir to measure ice thickness. There is a great deal of wind, and nothing to talk about for four miles. If your boots do not leak, you may come."

"My boots leak," Clara said.

Johan picked up the tin of dubbin from the floor and slid it across the table until it touched her wrist. "Then you had better grease them."

Going up the back stairs, she paused on the second-floor landing. Through Martin’s half-open door, she saw her cheap thrift-store scarf tangled around his bedpost. Down the hall, yellow light showed beneath Carl’s door, accompanied by the rhythmic *scritch-scritch* of his X-Acto knife. 

She waited for the familiar tightening in her chest, the anxious flutter of wanting to be drawn in red ink in the margins of their lives. Nothing happened. The hallway just smelled of old cabbage and damp plaster.

She retrieved her scarf without looking at Martin’s nightstand and climbed to the attic. Sitting on her bed in the cold room, she spread an old copy of the *Cleveland Plain Dealer* over the rug, and began, with great care and very little grace, to rub the yellow grease into the seams of her leather boots.
